newsitem.title: USA: Lilly shares off on margin, tax questions.
newsitem.headline: Lilly shares off on margin, tax questions.

text.p: Eli Lilly & Co shares moved down in late trading after fourth-quarter profit margins came in lower, and expenses higher, than Wall Street expected.
Lilly was down 2-1/2 to 80-3/8 late in Monday's session.
Gross margins were off and results were influenced by an unusual tax item, raising questions among analysts.
Still, said Cowen & Co analyst Steve Scala, "I'm not overly concerned."
Fourth-quarter gross margin was about 71.3 percent, down from about 72.5 percent in the year-ago period.

In a conference call, Lilly chief financial officer Charles Golden said the decline "primarily reflects the effects of PCS." Revenues from the company's PCS Health Systems unit, which has lower profit margins, rose to about $372 million from $259 million a year earlier.
"In the scope of the world, PCS is a little fly on Lilly," said Merrill Lynch drug industry analyst Richard Vietor.
"There are not as many issues here as the market seems to be saying," Vietor said of quarterly results.

Golden said: "Gross margins in our core pharmaceutical business, excluding PCS, will be expected to improve. And our SG&A expenses will continue to moderate and grow at a lower rate than our sales will grow for the full year."
Research and development expenses are expected to grow 14 to 17 percent in 1997, Golden said.
R&D expense for the fourth quarter was $349.4 million, up 23 percent over a year ago. Golden said the increase reflected late-stage trials for key drugs such as raloxifene.
"Raloxifene trials do remain on track," he said.

Results for the quarter and 1996 were also boosted by a strong other-income line, up to $12.6 million on the quarter and $273.3 million on the year, compared to $18.9 million and $70.1 million for the corresponding year-ago periods.
The rise came primarily on three deals last year involving sales of marketing rights to four Lilly drugs, Golden said.

Prozac sales on the quarter were lifted by wholesaler purchasing, Golden said. "We had a price increase in early 1997 on Prozac. And there tended to be, we think...some buy-ahead of that in the fourth quarter of 1996," he said.
Prozac sales are expected to grow at a rate roughly equal to that of anti-depressant market growth in 1997, Golden said.

The Indianapolis-based drugmaker's fourth-quarter earnings of $0.68 per share, versus $0.57 per share on an operating basis in the year-ago period, were exactly in line with analysts' expectations. "They just reported as expected, where maybe people were expecting them to do a little better," said independent analyst Hemant Shah.
